name: Camel milk
short: Raw camel milk: brucellosis outbreak (median age 10), a boy of 7, endocarditis. Hepatitis E after camel meat and milk (liver transplant). Allergy: anaphylaxis in 4 of 9. Autism: no adverse-event data.
text: Infection (outbreak and case reports, outside autism): brucellosis, a bacterial infection that causes fever and joint pain, has been traced to camel milk. In Qatar, 14 members of one rural family, with a median age of 10 years, developed brucellosis from the milk of an infected camel; all had fever, some with joint pain, weakness, headache, diarrhoea or abdominal pain, and their liver enzymes were raised. In southern Israel, 15 members of an extended Bedouin family (a population that, the authors note, consumes unpasteurised dairy products) developed acute brucellosis after drinking infected camel milk, and a later Israeli outbreak was traced by genome sequencing to commercially sold camel milk. A 7-year-old boy who had drunk raw camel milk, with no contact with animals, had brucellosis presenting as a painful chest-wall mass and was treated with surgery and three months of antibiotics. Three immigrants with brucellosis linked to camel milk (raw, as the title states) all had bacteria in the blood, and one had definite and one possible infection of the heart valves (endocarditis). In a cross-sectional study in southern Jordan, drinking raw camel milk daily was linked with antibodies to Brucella (adjusted odds ratio 2.19). Other infections: a liver transplant recipient from the Middle East who regularly consumed camel meat and milk had chronic infection with camel hepatitis E virus (a case report; meat and milk were both eaten, and the abstract does not say whether the milk was raw). In a rural Kenyan town, a case-control analysis among children and young adults found raw, boiled and fermented camel milk were each a risk factor for diarrhoea or vomiting (an association, alongside several other foods). Allergy: a retrospective review of nine patients (mean age 4.3 years) with camel milk allergy, which the authors call very rare, found hives and/or swelling (angioedema) in five and anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) in four, all within 15 minutes of drinking camel milk from the family farm; all had a family history of allergies and 77.8% had other allergies. Another record, with no abstract, is titled 'Anaphylaxis to camel milk in an atopic child'. In children with cow's milk allergy (a different group), 7 of 35 had a positive skin test to camel milk, and all with a negative test drank it without reactions; in a crossover trial in 15 children aged 1 to 18 with confirmed cow's milk allergy, none had adverse effects after camel milk. In another study of 67 children with cow's milk allergy, 21 had a positive skin test to camel milk (skin tests only; the abstract does not report drinking challenges). Autism: the abstract of a meta-analysis of five camel milk trials in children with autism, and the two trial abstracts cited on the autism page (one of which gave raw camel milk to one group), report no adverse-event data. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
